title: Cell structure
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for AQA GCSE Biology (8461) (status of the source: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms and clues: 4.1.1-c01 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.1.1-c10 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.1.1.1-xt2 term and clue written for the game; 4.1.1-c03 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.1.1-q01, 4.1.1-q03, 4.1.1-q02, 4.1.1-q04, 4.1.1-x01 (written for the game), 4.1.1-q05, 4.1.1-q06.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Eukaryotic cell
items.clue: A cell that has its genetic material enclosed in a nucleus.

items.label: Permanent vacuole
items.clue: A space in the cytoplasm of a plant cell that is filled with cell sap.

items.label: Cell membrane
items.clue: The thin outer boundary that controls what enters and leaves the cytoplasm

items.label: Plasmid
items.clue: A small ring of DNA in the cytoplasm of a bacterial cell, separate from the single DNA loop.

questions.stem: Which statement about a bacterial cell is correct?

options.text: Its genetic material is held inside a nucleus.
Its cell wall is made from cellulose fibres.
Its width is close to that of a cheek cell.
Its genetic material is a single DNA loop.

questions.explanation: The genetic material of a bacterial cell is not enclosed in a nucleus: it is a single DNA loop, and there may also be one or more small rings of DNA called plasmids.

questions.stem: A muscle cell contains large numbers of mitochondria. What is the function of these mitochondria?

options.text: To transfer energy by aerobic respiration
To make energy needed for contraction
To join amino acids into new proteins
To store the glucose used in exercise

questions.explanation: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place, transferring the energy the cell needs. A muscle cell needs a great deal of energy, so its structure includes many mitochondria.

questions.stem: A cheek cell is 6 × 10⁻⁵ m wide and a bacterial cell is 2 × 10⁻⁶ m wide. About how many times wider is the cheek cell?

options.text: About 3 times wider
About 300 times wider
About 30 times wider
About 0.03 times wider

questions.explanation: 6 × 10⁻⁵ divided by 2 × 10⁻⁶ is 3 × 10¹, so the cheek cell is about 30 times wider. This is the order of magnitude difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

questions.stem: Which parts are found in most animal cells?

options.text: Cytoplasm, ribosomes and a cellulose wall
Cytoplasm, mitochondria and cell sap
Cytoplasm, ribosomes and mitochondria
Cytoplasm, ribosomes and a large vacuole

questions.explanation: Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes, so all three parts listed here are present.

questions.stem: How is the genetic material of an animal cell different from that of a bacterial cell?

options.text: It is a single loop of DNA in the cytoplasm
It is enclosed inside a nucleus
It is found in small rings called plasmids
It is made of protein instead of DNA

questions.explanation: In animal cells the genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus; in bacteria it is a loop not in a nucleus.

questions.stem: Which statement about plant cells is correct?

options.text: Their cell walls are found in animals too.
Their cell walls are made of cellulose.
Their chloroplasts are in every plant cell.
Their vacuoles are found in animals too.

questions.explanation: Plant and algal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell.

questions.stem: A plant cell is 0.06 mm long. On a drawing of the cell, the nucleus is about one tenth of the length of the cell. What is the best estimate of the real diameter of the nucleus?

options.text: 0.6 mm

questions.explanation: The estimate from the drawing is that the nucleus is one tenth of the cell length, so its real diameter is 0.06 mm / 10 = 0.006 mm. This judges the relative size of a sub-cellular structure.
